% Introduction chapter -- revised March 2026, replaces the 2025 draft.
\section{Background}
The horse fairs of the Sichuan--Tibet corridor occupied a peculiar
position in the commercial geography of highland Asia. Neither purely
periodic markets nor permanent entrepots, they assembled for ten to
twenty days each autumn, drawing tea merchants from the Sichuan basin,
pastoralists from the Khams highlands, and brokers who moved between
the two worlds with fluency in both commercial idioms.

Imperial administrators regarded the fairs with ambivalence. The tea
and horse trade had been a state monopoly in earlier centuries, and the
revival of private dealing in the mid-eighteenth century forced
officials to choose between suppression and accommodation. County
archives show that most chose accommodation, taxing the fairs rather
than banning them, and in doing so created a paper trail of surprising
density.

Prices at the fairs were quoted in tea bricks rather than silver, a
practice that complicates comparison with lowland markets. A prime
gelding in 1780 fetched forty bricks of first-grade Ya'an tea; by 1820
the same animal cost sixty-five, a shift that contemporaries attributed
to declining tea quality as much as to horse scarcity.

\section{Research Questions}
This study asks three questions. First, how did the geography of the
fair network change between 1750 and 1850, and what does that movement
reveal about the shifting balance between state and private commerce?
Second, who bore the risk in horse--tea exchange, and how did contract
practice allocate losses when animals died in transit? Third, why did
tea-brick pricing persist long after silver had become common in other
highland trades?

These questions situate the fairs within a broader debate about
frontier institutions. Rather than treating the borderlands as a zone
of failed state penetration, the study follows recent work that reads
frontier markets as sites of institutional creativity, where officials,
merchants, and pastoralists improvised arrangements that none could
have imposed alone.

\section{Background}
The horse fairs of the Sichuan--Tibet corridor occupied a peculiar

and horse trade had been a state monopoly in earlier centuries, and the
revival of private dealing in the mid-eighteenth century forced
officials to choose between suppression and accommodation. County
archives show that most chose accommodation, taxing the fairs rather
than banning them, and in doing so created a paper trail of
considerable density.

\section{Aims of the Study}
This study asks how the geography of the fair network changed between
1750 and 1850, and what that movement reveals about the shifting
balance between state and private commerce. It also asks who bore the
risk in horse--tea exchange, and how contract practice allocated losses
when animals died in transit.

Prices at the fairs were quoted in tea bricks rather than silver. A
prime gelding in 1780 fetched forty bricks of first-grade Ya'an tea;

\section{Chapter Overview}
Chapter Two describes the archival base. Chapter Three reconstructs the
fair network from tax registers. Chapter Four analyses contract
practice, and Chapter Five concludes.

\section{Sources and Methods}
The evidentiary base of this study is the tax archive of three counties
through which the principal fair circuits passed. Registers of the fair
tax survive for most years between 1748 and 1852, recording the number
of horses presented, the tax assessed per head, and the surname and
native place of each seller.

These registers are supplemented by two bodies of material. The first
is a run of guild account books from a Ya'an tea firm, covering
1801--1840, which record purchases of horses for the caravan trade.
The second is the collected correspondence of a circuit intendant
whose district included two of the three counties, preserved in the
provincial archive.

Quantitative material is used sparingly. The registers undercount
private sales concluded away from the fairground, and no attempt is
made to extrapolate total trade volume from taxed volume. Where the
account books and the registers disagree, the disagreement is reported
rather than harmonised.
